overview: Phlebotomists draw blood for tests, transfusions, donations and research. They confirm each patient's identity, label tubes, match them to lab orders and safely dispose of needles. O*NET rates speaking at 3.5 out of 5 for this job and knowledge of customer service at 4.38, since calming nervous patients is part of every draw. Training is short, often a certificate program of a few months, followed by certification. The BLS May 2025 median is $45,230 across 143,540 jobs. The work is repetitive and on your feet, but hours are usually regular.
pay: Phlebotomists earn a median of $45,230, and the range is narrow: the middle half earn $38,190 to $48,930. California pays the most at $56,040, 24% above the national figure, and also has the most jobs, 13,520. Texas has 12,820 jobs at a median of $40,450.

faq.a: The BLS May 2025 median is $45,230 a year. The lowest 10% earn under $35,780 and the top 10% earn $58,780 or more. California, the District of Columbia and New York have the highest state medians, while Mississippi ($36,290) and Louisiana ($36,120) pay the least.

faq.q: How long does it take to become a phlebotomist?
faq.a: Most phlebotomy certificate programs take a few months to a year at a community college or technical school, and O*NET places the job in Job Zone 3. Most employers want national certification, which requires a set number of successful blood draws and an exam.

It is a quick way into health care with steady demand. In O*NET data the job ranks above 92% of U.S. jobs for repeating the same tasks and above 91% for working with people. Many use it as a first step toward nursing or lab careers.

Cardiovascular technologists are an 86% match and earn $74,310, 64% more. Radiologic technologists are an 81% match and earn $80,110, 77% more, according to BLS May 2025 data. Both usually need an associate degree, so they take longer to start.
